🇰🇷 South Korean words vs. 🇰🇵 North Korean words

1. 오빠 → 동지
South: “older brother,” also what women call a boyfriend. North: “comrade.” Calling a boyfriend oppa is banned there since 2023.

2. 진짜 → 참말
South: “for real.” North: “true words.”

3. 드라마 → 연속극
South: from English “drama.” North: “continuous play.” English loanwords are avoided.

4. 라면 → 꼬부랑국수
South: instant noodles. North: “curly noodles.”

5. 치킨 → 닭튀기
South: from English “chicken.” North: “fried chicken” in pure Korean.

6. 햄버거 → 다진소고기겹빵
South: “hamburger.” North: “minced beef layered bread.”

7. 아이스크림 → 얼음보숭이 (또는 에스키모)
South: “ice cream.” North: “ice fluff,” though most just say Eskimo.

8. 스킨 → 살결물
South: Konglish for facial toner. North: “skin-texture water.”

9. 담배 → 구름과자
Both: 담배 means cigarette. 구름과자, “cloud snack,” is a playful nickname used on both sides.

10. 남자친구/여자친구 → 연애동무
South: boyfriend/girlfriend. North: “romance comrade.”

11. 핸드폰 → 손전화
South: Konglish “hand phone.” North: “hand telephone.”

Which one surprised you most? 👇

CUPED is a common way to reduce variance in A/B tests, and it’s very likely to come up in a data science interview. The usual version adjusts each market by its own pre-period metric, which can miss who actually shows up during the test.

I simulated a 60-market Airbnb experiment based on a recent Instacart post. Predicting each booking and averaging up to the market removed about half the variance, compared to 28% for standard CUPED.

Knowing that the covariate only needs to be unaffected by the treatment is the kind of follow-up that helps senior and staff data scientists stand out. Full tutorial and Colab notebook at the link in bio.

What does 666 actually mean?

Most people treat Revelation like a horror movie. They panic over the number and every scary headline.

The book’s very first verse tells you who it’s about. It’s the revelation of Jesus Christ (Revelation 1:1).

Revelation 13:18 says, “Here is wisdom. Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man; and his number is Six hundred threescore and six.”

Six represents man, and 666 warns us about what happens when man tries to take God’s place.

Satan builds what I call an unholy trinity, a fake version of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit with man sitting where God belongs. Each six is one of those seats.

The first is the Father’s seat as judge. We sit in it every time we decide what we deserve and what everybody else deserves.

With the second six, we push aside the Holy Spirit, who comforts and leads us, and numb the pain with whatever we reach for instead of bringing it to God.

The last six puts us in the Son’s seat as Savior. That’s legalism, trying to make ourselves right with God by what we do. Ephesians 2:8-9 says, “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”

Understanding 666 shouldn’t leave you fascinated with Satan. It should expose the places where you’ve put yourself on God’s throne and send you back to Jesus.

Those seats still belong to Him.

On a summer evening in Boston, something remarkable happened in the American story. When Barack Obama walked onto the stage at the Democratic National Convention, he was not yet president or a household name, but there was a feeling that history was beginning to pay attention. His words carried more than ambition; they carried hope and faith in a country capable of overcoming its divisions and living up to the promises of its founding. In that moment, regardless of where people came from or which side they supported, they could feel the spirit of America growing stronger.
He spoke about unity in a way that felt genuine, not forced or simply designed to win applause, but inspired by something much deeper. He reminded Americans that the country was not divided into separate red and blue states, but united as one nation through shared dreams, challenges, and aspirations. For many people watching that night, his message was a powerful reminder of what America could be at its best: a place where opportunity is not limited to a privileged few, but available to anyone willing to work hard, dream big, and believe in a better future. It was the kind of speech that made people stand a little taller and feel proud of the nation they called home.
Looking back, that speech was more than just a moment in a political campaign; it was the beginning of something significant. It reminded people that leadership is not simply about holding power, but about serving a greater purpose. It showed that patriotism does not have to be loud or boastful, but can be expressed through quiet determination, lasting hope, and the belief that tomorrow can be better than today. On July 27, 2004, in Boston, Barack Obama reminded the nation that America’s story was far from finished, and that every generation has the opportunity to continue writing it with courage, conviction, and faith in the country they call home.

During the Korean War in 1950, Turkish soldier Süleyman Dilbirliği discovered a five-year-old Korean girl, Kim Eun-ja, who had been orphaned by the conflict. He took her into his care named her Ayla, and looked after her as his own daughter for more than a year. When he was ordered to return to Turkey, they were forced to separate, and Ayla was placed in an orphanage.

For decades, they lost contact until they were finally reunited in South Korea in 2010, nearly 60 years after their separation. In December 2017, Ayla returned to Turkey to see him one last time, shortly before he passed away aged 91.

That’s what humility really is. Not thinking less of yourself, but being so sure of who you are that you can let someone else shine.

Insecure people need to win every battle. Humble people know when to let someone else have the moment.

Win where it counts. Let go where it doesn’t.

Chia seeds + water = a pita pocket? 👀🥑

Just two ingredients for the pita. No flour, no eggs. Add shrimp, mango, avocado, and a squeeze of lime, and lunch is ready.

INGREDIENTS

For the pita:
• 60 g chia seeds
• 250 ml water

For the filling:
• cooked, cooled shrimp
• mango
• avocado
• tomatoes
• onion
• garlic
• cilantro
• jalapeño
• fresh lime juice
• salt to taste

HOW TO MAKE IT

1. Mix the chia seeds with the water and let sit for at least 1 hour, until a thick gel forms.
2. Heat a dry nonstick skillet. Spoon in the mixture and spread it into even, round flatbreads.
3. Cook for about 10 minutes, flipping frequently, until firm enough to hold their shape. They may puff up, flatten, and puff again as they cook.
4. Let cool slightly, then carefully snip open the top with kitchen scissors to create a pocket.
5. Chop the filling ingredients and gently mix with salt and fresh lime juice. Add as much jalapeño as you like.
6. Fill the pita pockets and serve immediately.

Crisp edges, juicy shrimp, creamy avocado, and sweet mango with a little heat 🌶️

Save the recipe for your next lunch, and tell me: what would you put inside? 🤍
